title: Every night, all of history again
teaches: Deterministic replay, a job scheduler with leases and retries, a million tasks on a shared cluster (Borg), preemptible capacity, versioned datasets, and comparing results

blocks.text: When id Software released *Doom* in December 1993, players could record a game and send it to a friend as a **demo**, a file of a few kilobytes. A demo held no video frames at all. The game advances in steps called **tics**, at 35 tics per second, and the demo held only what the player pressed in each tic, such as forward, turn, or fire. Playing it back ran the whole game again from the same start, feeding in the same inputs. Because every part of the game was **deterministic**, the same inputs produced the same monsters in the same places and the same shots landing on the same tics. Even the game's random numbers came from a fixed table of 256 values, read in order.[^rnd] Demos had a known weakness. When played on a different version of the game where some rule had changed by a fraction, they **desynced**. The player's recorded inputs carried on into a world that had drifted, and the replayed marine walked into walls.

Twenty-two years later, Abhishek Verma and colleagues at Google described Borg, the cluster manager that had run nearly all of Google's work for a decade (EuroSys, April 2015). A Borg **cell** was a set of machines managed as a single unit, with a median size of about 10,000 machines. Production jobs, the services that respond to users, ran at high priority. Batch jobs, such as analyses, builds, and tests, ran at low priority on whatever capacity production left unused, and were **preempted** (stopped and moved) whenever production needed the capacity back. Each cell's controller, the Borgmaster, was replicated five times and maintained its state through Paxos, the consensus protocol from lesson 11.

In this lesson, we will combine both ideas in a design exercise. The fleet of survey vehicles from lesson D5 runs onboard software that decides what data to keep and tags what it detects. We must check every change to that software against **a million recorded scenarios** of 30 seconds each, selected from the catalogue. Every night, we must compare the new build against the current one and deliver the results to engineers by 07:00. We will design the system that runs this workload, and then compare it with systems published by Google and others.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional requirements.** We need to run a software build against a named set of scenarios, both on a schedule and on demand. We will split each run into a directed graph of tasks: simulate, score, compare, and report. The system must retry a task if its host machine fails, and stop retrying a task that fails deterministically on every attempt. It must compare each scenario's result with the same scenario under the baseline build and report regressions. Finally, we must construct scenario sets from catalogue queries and save each set as an immutable, named version.

**Non-functional requirements.** Results must arrive by 07:00. Runs must be **reproducible** so that running the same build on the same scenario yields the exact same result, bit for bit, next week or next year; otherwise, engineers cannot trust a reported difference. A machine failure should cost minutes of lost work rather than an entire night. The run should remain inexpensive by using spare cluster capacity, and one team's workload must not starve another's.
**Out of scope.** We will not cover the simulator's physics and sensor models, the catalogue and storage systems from lesson D5, or the code review and build systems that supply the binaries to test.

parts.title: The same inputs, the same answer

blocks.text: A replay is useful only if it is exact. Before we design the system, examine how a tiny numerical change affects a replay.

blocks.caption: A puck steered by recorded inputs among round pegs, recorded once and replayed three ways. Grey is the recorded run; the coloured line is the replay.
blocks.task: Guess, then replay with the new build that rounds to 32 bits

blocks.text: With the same build and the same random seed, the replay matches the recorded run across all 600 tics, which at *Doom*'s rate of 35 tics per second is about 17 seconds of activity. If you change one unrecorded variable, such as drawing a random number from a different seed, the trajectories diverge within a few dozen tics. If you change only the floating-point rounding by one part in ten million, the trajectories track together briefly before diverging completely. Each collision with a curved peg multiplies a small positional error by several times, so a discrepancy of 0.0000001 requires only about ten collisions to span the entire width of the box. Real driving scenes contain similar thresholds: a detector's confidence score falling just above or below a cutoff, an object being tracked or dropped, or a control decision occurring one tic earlier.

Therefore, engineers build the simulator to be strictly deterministic, and record or pin every input. The simulator uses a simulated **clock** rather than the host machine's system clock. It draws random numbers from a seeded pseudoranom generator, storing the seed alongside the scenario. Because threads may execute in any order, the simulator combines thread outputs in a fixed sequence and performs floating-point additions (which are not associative) in a single deterministic order. We pin the software build using the cryptographic hash of its binaries and libraries. Each run logs the hash of every input, and an automated nightly test verifies that a small sample of the previous night's runs produces identical output bytes. If a run diverges, engineers inspect the first tic where the outputs differ.

Two kinds of replay serve different testing needs. In **open-loop** replay, the system feeds recorded sensor data into the new build and compares its outputs. This suffices for passive software that only observes, such as perception detectors and data-logging triggers. Software that controls the vehicle alters future states, and a static recording cannot react when the vehicle steers differently; the recorded world continues as if the original software were still in control. Testing control software requires **closed-loop** simulation, where the simulator models the surrounding actors and makes them respond to the vehicle. Both modes require determinism, though closed-loop simulation is more sensitive because any small discrepancy feeds back into the next tic's state.

blocks.caption: The estimate for a nightly run, at one core-second for each simulated second.
blocks.task: Guess, then make the simulator slower

blocks.text: One million 30-second scenarios equal 347 days of driving. At a processing rate of 1 core-second per simulated second, a full run requires about 8,333 core-hours, which finishes in under an hour on 10,000 CPU cores. A full sensor simulation runs several times slower, at roughly 4 core-seconds per simulated second, and comparing builds requires running the baseline build as well. Calculating 2 × 1,000,000 × 30 s × 4 core-seconds per second gives 240,000,000 core-seconds, or about 67,000 core-hours per night. Purchasing dedicated machines for this workload would leave them idle during the day, so we run the batch job overnight when interactive cluster usage drops.

The false-positive rate in our estimate is equally important. If an individual comparison flags a regression by chance 1% of the time, one million comparisons will generate 10,000 false alarms every night, which is far too many for engineers to review. We must design the statistical comparison as carefully as the execution engine, as we will see later in this lesson.

parts.title: A scheduler that survives its machines

blocks.text: We will coordinate the workload using a **job scheduler**, a distributed equivalent of Unix's cron. Its HTTP API provides three main operations. To submit a job, a client sends `POST /jobs` with a name, a cron schedule such as `0 22 * * *` (22:00 every day), the target build and scenario set, the task dependency graph, a priority level, and the team quota to bill. To monitor progress, a client calls `GET /jobs/{id}/runs` to list each run and the states of its tasks. A third endpoint stops a running job. All state resides in a **job store**, a small replicated database containing one row per job with its next scheduled run time, one row per run, and one row per task. Each task row records its execution state, its attempt count, its upstream task dependencies, and a **lease** specifying which worker holds the task and when that lease expires.

During any nightly run, hardware will fail and the cluster manager will preempt thousands of workers. Before looking at the architecture diagram, consider how the scheduler should assign tasks to workers. You might consider four approaches: send each task to a worker and assume it finishes; guarantee that each task executes exactly once; send every task to two workers simultaneously; or let a worker hold a task under a time-limited lease that it periodically renews, reassigning the task if the lease expires. Test which approach survives the failure modes below.

blocks.caption: How should a scheduler make sure every task runs, when workers die?
blocks.task: Guess, then show the clues one by one

options.guess: Which way of handing out tasks works?

ideas.name: Fire and forget
ideas.text: Hand each task to a worker and move on to the next.

ideas.name: Exactly once
ideas.text: Make sure each task runs once, and never a second time.

ideas.name: Everything twice
ideas.text: Send every task to two workers and keep whichever answer arrives first.

ideas.name: Leases and retries
ideas.text: A worker holds a task for a few minutes at a time and renews the hold; if the hold runs out, another worker takes the task.

clues.name: Workers die
clues.text: Disks and machines fail every day in a large cell (lesson 7), and preemption stops thousands of tasks a night.

clues.name: Dead or slow
clues.text: A worker that stops answering may be dead, paused, or cut off from the network; nothing can tell the scheduler which (lesson 11).

clues.name: Twice the bill
clues.text: Running every task twice doubles 67,000 core-hours a night, and the extra copies take room the first copies need.

clues.name: Named by inputs
clues.text: Each task writes its result under the hash of all its inputs, so a second run writes the same bytes to the same name.

options.end: Leases give at least once. Results named by their inputs make a second run harmless, which is as good as exactly once.

blocks.caption: The scheduler's parts. Workers pull tasks from the store; the elected scheduler only decides what is due.

blocks.text: The **scheduler** runs as a single active process elected via a distributed lock service (as in lesson 11), with standby instances waiting to take over. Once a minute, the active scheduler queries the job store for jobs whose scheduled run time has passed and inserts a run record for each, keyed by the job ID and scheduled timestamp. If a newly elected leader repeats the check for that same minute, this unique key prevents it from creating a duplicate run. The scheduler also transitions tasks to the **ready** state once all of their upstream dependencies complete; because tasks form a directed graph, the simulate task must finish before the score task can begin. The scheduler never pushes tasks directly to workers. Instead, workers **pull** work by querying the store for a ready task and claiming it with an atomic conditional write (the same mechanism used to prevent double-booking seats in lesson D4, *Fourteen million people, two million tickets*). This write sets the task's lease holder to the worker's ID and sets the expiration timestamp to five minutes in the future. The worker renews this lease every minute while executing the task.[^lease]

If a worker crashes, its lease expires and the task returns to the ready state for another worker to claim. If a worker merely pauses (for example, due to a network partition or garbage-collection pause) and resumes after its lease expires, it might finish a task that a second worker has already completed. Because the system executes each task **at least once**, we must make every task **idempotent** so that duplicate executions do not corrupt the state. Workers write each task's output to storage using the cryptographic hash of the task's inputs as the filename, so overwriting the file produces the exact same bytes. The task's attempt counter acts as a fencing token (from lesson 11): if a lease expires and increments the task to attempt 3, the database rejects a status update from the slow worker still holding attempt 2. When a task fails with an error, the system retries it with exponential backoff up to three attempts before marking it permanently failed and logging it in the morning report. Without a retry limit, a single corrupted scenario that crashes the simulator deterministically would retry forever and consume cluster capacity.

Two additional rules keep scheduled jobs predictable. First, if the scheduler is offline at 22:00, it triggers the **missed run** once upon recovery rather than launching a separate run for every minute it was down. Second, jobs enforce **priorities** and **quotas**. In Borg, each team received a resource quota for each priority band; the system rejected jobs that exceeded their quota at submission time rather than queueing them indefinitely, and allowed higher-priority tasks to preempt lower-priority ones.[^bands]

Consider a cluster cell of 15,000 CPU cores that serves interactive user traffic all day, peaking at 14:00. Our nightly simulation batch job starts at 22:00 and must finish by 07:00. We can either reserve dedicated cores at production priority, or run at batch priority using spare capacity left by production services, accepting that our tasks will be preempted whenever production traffic rises. We must also choose the task duration. Every task spends 1 minute starting up to fetch the build binary and load the scenario data, and batch tasks face random preemption at an average rate of 20% per hour.

blocks.caption: One night on a shared cell. Production's use rises and falls through the day; the run fills what is left, or a reservation. Prices are round figures of our own.
blocks.task: Finish by 07:00 on preemptible cores, wasting under a tenth

blocks.text: Reserving 4,000 dedicated cores costs about $3,840 per day regardless of utilisation, and still finishes running both builds at 15:48, nearly nine hours past the 07:00 deadline. Preemptible batch capacity costs a quarter as much per core-hour and provides twice as many available cores overnight. However, if we group work into two-hour tasks without checkpointing, preemption wastes a quarter of our total core-hours. At a preemption rate of 20% per hour, a two-hour task is interrupted 0.4 times on average, and each interruption loses an average of one hour of progress, wasting 20% of all compute work. When morning production traffic ramps up, the cluster preempts thousands of additional batch tasks simultaneously, raising total wasted work to 25%. Conversely, sizing tasks too small wastes capacity on startup overhead: a two-minute task spends half its runtime loading binaries and data. Sizing tasks between 20 and 30 minutes balances startup overhead against preemption losses. Adding periodic checkpoints changes this trade-off: if a task saves its state to storage every five minutes, a preemption loses at most five minutes of compute work, making multi-hour tasks viable.

We can achieve an even larger reduction in compute time by eliminating redundant runs. Because the baseline build already ran the previous night against the exact same scenarios, its outputs are already stored under the hashes of their inputs. If workers query the storage cache for an existing input hash before running the simulator, we skip the baseline simulations entirely, and the nightly job finishes shortly after 02:00. Build systems apply this same technique to source code: Bazel, which Google open-sourced in 2015, maintains a **remote cache** of build artifacts keyed by the cryptographic hash of all compilation inputs, ensuring that an unchanged source file compiled on one workstation is never recompiled on another.[^hash]

Borg increased cluster utilisation further through resource **reclamation**. Because engineers provision production jobs with extra capacity to handle traffic spikes, Borg continuously estimated each production task's actual resource consumption and scheduled batch tasks inside the unused allocation. If a production task's traffic spiked and the estimate proved too low, Borg immediately preempted those batch tasks to reclaim the capacity.

parts.title: The night the leader went away

blocks.text: Alongside the nightly batch run, the job store manages smaller recurring jobs, such as an hourly job that replays scenarios flagged by engineers during the day. Suppose the machine hosting the active scheduler loses power at 03:00. Its session in the distributed lock service expires about 10 seconds later. A standby scheduler acquires the lock, receives a new **epoch** number incremented by one above the old leader's epoch, and reads the current state from the job store. The scheduler attaches its epoch number to every database write, and the job store rejects any write carrying a stale epoch. As covered in lesson 11, this fencing mechanism ensures that if the previous leader was merely paused and later resumes, it cannot corrupt the job state. Because the old leader held no authoritative state in local memory, the new leader loses no context. If the old leader already inserted the run record for the 03:00 hourly job before crashing, the new leader sees the record in the database; if not, the new leader inserts it, relying on the unique composite key of job ID and scheduled timestamp to prevent duplicate runs. Meanwhile, the roughly 9,000 active workers (one per CPU core allocated to the batch run at 03:00) continue uninterrupted. Because workers communicate directly with the job store rather than the scheduler, they continue renewing leases and claiming ready tasks, delaying only those downstream tasks whose dependencies completed during the 10-second failover window.

At 03:20 the job store itself loses one of its five replicas. With four left it still has a majority, as lesson 11 showed, and carries on. Had the store been one database on one machine, the whole night's run would have stopped until someone repaired it, which is why the store, not the scheduler, is the part replicated with Paxos. Keep the store small, rows about tasks and never the results themselves, and five copies of it are cheap.

At 04:10, a scenario recorded in heavy snow triggers a crash in the new software build. The worker marks the attempt failed, and the task waits for its backoff timer, fails a second time, and is marked permanently failed after its third attempt. At 07:00, the morning report highlights this crash at the top of the summary alongside the build hash, the scenario ID, and the exact simulation tic where the process terminated, allowing engineers to turn the scenario into a permanent regression test.

Each completed scenario task outputs quantitative metrics: how many obstacles the software detected and at what distance, how frequently a data-collection trigger fired, and the positional error of tracked vehicles relative to ground truth. Comparing the new build against the baseline across one million scenarios produces one million slight numerical differences. Because the simulator is deterministic, every difference is genuine rather than random run-to-run noise; re-running the build will produce the exact same numbers. However, a genuine difference is not necessarily a meaningful regression. As shown in our earlier pegboard simulation, any code change alters floating-point trajectories across thousands of scenarios, nudging metrics slightly higher in some scenes and slightly lower in others.

To separate systematic regressions from trajectory jitter, engineers aggregate results in layers. First, the reporting pipeline groups scenarios by their catalogue metadata tags, such as `night`, `rain`, `cyclists`, or `junctions`. For each group, the report calculates the failure rate under both builds and computes a statistical confidence interval for the difference between the two proportions, estimating how much the rate could fluctuate due to sample variance across similar scenes. This statistical test also dictates the minimum group size: detecting a failure rate increase from 1.0% to 1.2% requires roughly 16 × p(1 − p) ÷ (difference)² scenarios, which evaluates to 16 × 0.01 × 0.99 ÷ 0.002², or about 40,000 scenarios per group. The report flags a group only when its metric shift exceeds the confidence interval. Because evaluating hundreds of tag groups simultaneously guarantees that some groups will cross a standard threshold by chance, the pipeline adjusts the significance threshold to account for multiple hypothesis testing.[^fdr] Separately, the pipeline enforces strict invariants on every individual scenario: zero process crashes, and zero missed detections on objects marked critical by human annotators. Engineers then inspect the flagged groups and invariant failures using a visual debugger that replays the scenario side by side under both builds.

Valid comparisons require immutable test datasets. When an engineer defines a scenario set using a catalogue query such as `tags: night AND cyclist; recorded before 2026-10-01`, the system resolves that query into an explicit list of log segment IDs and their content hashes, saving the manifest as an immutable **version** named `night-cyclists@v7`. That version never changes; appending newly recorded driving logs creates `night-cyclists@v8`. The database records every simulation result alongside the exact dataset version, build hash, and simulator version. This provenance allows engineers in June to reproduce a regression first reported in March, or to run last year's software build against this year's scenario dataset to determine whether a failure mode was introduced by recent code changes or simply exposed by newer driving logs.

Borg's design is close to the one above, at a larger scale. Its paper describes cells of about 10,000 machines, each run by a Borgmaster replicated five times with Paxos, and a separate scheduler that reads the master's state and assigns tasks. Priority bands separated monitoring, production, batch and best effort work, with quotas per band, and preemption flowing only downwards. Most of a cell's batch work ran in reclaimed resources. Google's earlier MapReduce had shown the task-level ideas in 2004 (lesson 8): a master that re-runs the tasks of a dead worker, outputs written so a duplicate is harmless, and backup copies of the slowest tasks near the end of a job.

These patterns are standard across the industry. Apache Airflow, created at Airbnb and open-sourced in 2015, popularised scheduled task graphs where each job run is keyed by its scheduled timestamp, allowing operators to populate historical intervals or catch up on missed schedules through a process Airflow calls backfilling. Video game studios still rely on *Doom*-style deterministic input logs to reproduce bugs and run automated nightly playtests across hours of recorded inputs. Similarly, autonomous vehicle and robotics teams run nightly simulation suites against millions of scenarios extracted from fleet logs.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **At ten times the scale** (10 million scenarios), the nightly run consumes 670,000 core-hours, exceeding the spare overnight capacity of a single cluster cell. We must distribute the run across multiple cells and datacentres, adding a global routing layer above the cell schedulers to place jobs and pre-staging build binaries and scenario files in storage near each target cell. Because the job store's task table now accumulates tens of millions of rows per night, we partition the table by run ID and configure workers to claim and renew tasks in batches of 10 or 100 to reduce database write throughput. Storing full simulation outputs for every task becomes prohibitively expensive, so workers write only summary metrics for passing scenarios and retain full tic-by-tic telemetry logs exclusively for scenarios that fail an invariant or belong to a flagged regression group.

**A hundred times** is a bill no one pays every night. The design stops running everything and starts choosing. Each scenario records which parts of the software it exercises, and a change runs first against the scenarios that touch the code it changed. A **stratified sample**, a fixed number of scenes drawn from each group, sized as above, runs nightly; the full library runs weekly. And simulation itself comes in tiers, a fast low-fidelity one to screen every change and the full sensor simulation only for the changes that pass.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on running and reading a million replays
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A *Doom* demo recorded on one version of the game desyncs on another. Why?
choices: The demo holds only inputs, and the new version's game logic differs slightly
The demo file was compressed differently by the second version, and some of the recorded inputs were lost on loading
The second version ran at a different number of tics a second
items.why: Replaying recorded inputs reproduces a run only if the simulation logic is identical; a tiny change in rules compounds tic by tic.

items.ask: A replay of the same build and scenario gives a slightly different result each time. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The scenario's recording has been corrupted on disk, and so it is read back differently each time
Something the run depends on wasn't recorded or pinned, so it differs from one run to the next
The simulator is too slow, and its results change when the scheduler gives it more cores
items.why: Bit-for-bit replay needs every input fixed. Look for what the run reads that the recording didn't capture.

items.ask: A worker pauses for ten minutes, its lease expires, and another worker runs the same task. Then the first wakes and finishes too. What keeps the result correct?
choices: The scheduler kills the paused worker's machine at once
The second worker first checks with the first that it has stopped, and waits until it hears back
Results named by their inputs, and a fencing token on each attempt's writes
items.why: Because a distributed system cannot distinguish a paused worker from a crashed one, tasks execute at least once, and idempotent storage keys plus fencing tokens make duplicate runs harmless.

items.ask: The elected scheduler fails at 03:00 and a standby takes over. What does the standby need from the old leader?
choices: Nothing: every job, run, task and lease is in the replicated job store, which outlives any one leader
A copy of the old leader's memory, so that it knows which tasks were handed to which of the workers
A list of the workers, so that it can ask each one in turn what it is doing at the moment
items.why: Storing all state in the replicated database allows a standby scheduler to take over in seconds. Because workers pull tasks directly from the store, they continue executing during leader failover.

items.ask: On preemptible cores, two-hour tasks with no checkpoints waste about a quarter of the core-hours. What fixes it?
choices: Raising the run to production priority, so that it is never preempted, and paying for that
Tasks of 20 to 30 minutes, or checkpoints, so a preemption loses little work
Tasks of one minute, so that no task can ever be preempted part of the way through its work
items.why: Preemption discards any progress since the task started or last saved a checkpoint, while every task incurs a 1-minute startup cost. Sizing tasks to 20–30 minutes or writing periodic checkpoints balances both overheads.

items.ask: Comparing two builds on a million scenarios flags 10,000 changes, a 1% rate. What should the report do?
choices: Send all 10,000 to the engineers, since determinism means every one of the differences is real
Ignore all of them, since the simulator is too sensitive to small changes to be any use
Group the changes and compare each group's rate, with thresholds corrected for many tests
items.why: While determinism guarantees every numerical difference is real, most are harmless trajectory shifts in both directions. Comparing failure rates across tagged groups with multiple-testing corrections isolates systematic regressions, while strict invariants catch individual crashes.

items.ask: Why is a scenario set stored as a frozen version such as `night-cyclists@v7`?
choices: So builds and months are compared on exactly the same scenes
So that the catalogue's query runs faster the second time someone asks it, from a cache
So that the scenarios take less storage space than the raw logs that they were taken from
items.why: Re-running a live catalogue query weeks later will return newly uploaded logs, so freezing an immutable version manifest is necessary to make build comparisons and bug reports reproducible.

summary: **Deterministic replay requires pinning every input.** Replace the system clock with a simulated clock, seed all random number generators, enforce a fixed reduction order for floating-point sums, and pin software builds by cryptographic hash.

**Tiny numerical differences compound rapidly.** A rounding difference of one part in ten million diverges into an entirely different trajectory after a few collisions, so engineers evaluate builds by aggregated outcome metrics rather than exact paths.

**Estimate capacity requirements before provisioning hardware.** One million 30-second scenarios equal 347 days of driving; running two builds through a 4-core-second simulator requires roughly 67,000 core-hours per night.

**Store scheduler state in a small replicated database.** An elected leader inserts scheduled runs and resolves task dependencies, while workers pull ready tasks directly from the store using time-limited leases.

**Combine at-least-once execution with idempotent outputs.** Expired leases cause duplicate task runs, which remain safe when workers write outputs under input hashes and validate attempt numbers as fencing tokens. Cap retries to prevent poison-pill tasks from exhausting the cluster.

**Run batch workloads on preemptible spare capacity.** Spare overnight capacity is inexpensive; sizing tasks to 20–30 minutes or checkpointing state minimises preemption waste, while priority quotas prevent resource starvation.
**Cache results by the hash of their inputs.** Looking up existing simulation outputs in a content-addressed cache eliminates the baseline build run and cuts nightly compute work in half.

**Aggregate metrics across frozen dataset versions.** Group scenarios by metadata tags, test failure-rate shifts using thresholds adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing, enforce strict crash invariants on every scene, and pin datasets as immutable versions.

rnd.title: Doom's random numbers
rnd.text: *Doom*'s source code, released in 1997, contains a 256-byte array named `rndtable` and a lookup function that advances an index to return the next entry on each call. Gameplay simulation and cosmetic visual effects read from separate index pointers (`prndindex` and `rndindex`), ensuring that rendering an extra puff of smoke on a player's screen never altered monster behaviour. Starting a demo reset both indices to zero.

bands.title: Priority bands
bands.text: The Borg paper defines four non-overlapping priority bands: monitoring, production, batch, and best-effort (also called gratis or free). A high-priority task could preempt tasks in lower bands, but never a task within its own band, preventing cascading preemption chains among production services. Teams held separate resource quotas for each band, while best-effort tasks required no quota.

hash.title: Keys made of inputs
hash.text: A cache keyed by the hash of every input, code, data, parameters and tool versions, can never return a stale answer: change anything and the key changes. The risk runs the other way. An input left out of the key, such as an environment variable the simulator reads, lets two different runs share one key, and the cache returns the wrong result with complete confidence.

fdr.title: Many tests at once
fdr.text: With a threshold of 1%, a hundred groups with no real change still flag one on average. The Bonferroni correction divides the threshold by the number of tests, which is safe but misses real changes. The method of Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg (1995) controls instead the share of flagged results that are false, and is the usual choice when thousands of comparisons are read at once.

lease.title: Why five minutes
lease.text: Choosing a lease duration balances recovery latency against database write load. A short lease detects crashed workers quickly, but requires frequent heartbeats: 6,000 active workers renewing a lease every 10 seconds generate 600 writes per second on the job store solely for lease maintenance. A long lease reduces database load, but leaves a crashed worker's task idle until the timer expires. A 5-minute lease renewed every 60 seconds suits batch tasks that run for 20 to 30 minutes.
